title: Rights and Responsibilities in Client Care
introduction: Effective maternal and child health nursing rests on understanding both what clients are entitled to expect and what responsibilities clients and nurses share. Balancing legal and ethical rights, the Patients' Bill of Rights, the ICN fundamental nursing responsibilities, and four spheres of nursing accountability safeguards client dignity while protecting practitioners from liability.
learningOutcomes: 5.1 Define rights and obligations and distinguish legal rights from ethical rights in health care.
5.2 Trace the emergence of the Patients' Bill of Rights (AHA 1973/1992) and summarize the National Health Council (1995) Principles of Patients' Rights and Responsibilities.
5.3 Outline specific client rights and responsibilities in clinical settings and the nine principal areas of a Patients' Bill of Rights.
5.4 Explain the four fundamental ICN responsibilities of nurses and distinguish the four areas of nursing accountability for registered nurses versus student nurses.
5.5 Apply the Client's Bill of Rights practically to bedside nursing care, confidentiality, cultural sensitivity, graded self-care, and co-worker safety.

content.heading: Concept of Rights and Obligations: Legal vs. Ethical Rights
content.body: A right is a claim to a particular privilege (for example, someone who has paid for health care has a right to receive it). Rights are either legal or ethical. A legal right is an entitlement enforceable within the limits of law that co-exists with an obligation—the willingness to accept the burden, rewards, and risks of a given duty; violating a legal right exposes an individual to civil or criminal liability. An ethical right imposes a moral obligation on professionals to serve those who seek and pay for care, yet carries no statutory guarantee because no legal authority compels its enforcement (for instance, in Nigeria no law mandates employment or dictates whether a citizen visits an orthodox hospital, herbalist, or prayer home). Violating an ethical right results not in criminal prosecution, but in professional sanctions such as reprimand, censure, suspension, or expulsion. Heightened societal scrutiny of moral conduct has produced formal charters including Human Rights Bills, Rights of the Child, and Patients' Bills of Rights.

content.heading: Evolution of Client Rights and National Health Council (1995) Principles
content.body: The client rights movement emerged in the late 1960s with two broad goals: improving health care quality and making health systems more responsive to increasingly informed clients amid rapid scientific and technological expansion. In response, the American Hospital Association (AHA) published the first Patient's Bill of Rights in 1973 (revised in 1992). In January 1995, the National Health Council Board of Directors approved six Principles of Patients' Rights: (a) informed consent in treatment decisions, courteous dignified care, second opinions, timely specialty referrals, medical record confidentiality, and respect for legal advance directives/living wills; (b) concise, understandable information on health coverage, benefits, authorizations, and restrictions (supported by patient ombudsmen); (c) transparency in coverage payment decisions ('medically necessary' criteria) and fair, open appeals; (d) complete cost information covering premiums, deductibles, co-payments, and service fees; (e) reasonable choice of providers with access to credentials and accreditation data; and (f) disclosure of provider payment structures, financial incentives, conflicts of interest, or clinical rules affecting care.

content.heading: Specific Patient Rights, Responsibilities, and Principal Areas
content.body: In everyday clinical care, clients have the right to courteous, non-discriminatory treatment respecting race, ethnicity, national origin, gender, sexual orientation, religion, personal values, age, disability, and economic or veteran status; to choose or change providers and seek second opinions or referrals; to receive complete diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis information in understandable language (with confidential interpreters if needed); to participate in care decisions and give prior consent; to decline treatment as permitted by law after learning consequences; to expect strict privacy and confidentiality (records released only with written permission, court order, mandatory reporting of communicable diseases or child abuse, or preventing physical danger); and to review their health records. Correspondingly, patients hold four broad responsibilities (recognizing physical or mental illness may limit capacity): pursuing healthy lifestyles (good diet, rest, exercise; avoiding tobacco, excess alcohol, drug abuse), understanding their health plans, actively participating in care decisions, and cooperating with mutually accepted treatments. Practical client responsibilities (e.g., Gannett guidelines) include giving accurate health/medication/OTC/allergy histories, asking clarifying questions, completing regimens and follow-ups, keeping or promptly cancelling appointments, disclosing advance directives, arranging a 24-hour escort when required, managing insurance/billing honestly, respecting staff and other clients, and voicing concerns (or escalating unresolved grievances to accrediting bodies like AAAHC). Overall, a Patients' Bill of Rights covers nine principal areas: information disclosure, choice of providers and plans, access to emergency services, participation in treatment, respect and non-discrimination, confidentiality of health information, complaints, consumer responsibilities, and access to the full bill.

content.heading: Nurses' Fundamental Responsibilities and Four Areas of Accountability
content.body: Responsibility is an obligation to perform an act for which one becomes accountable. The International Council of Nurses (ICN) Code defines four fundamental responsibilities of nurses toward all people without discrimination: (1) to promote health, (2) to prevent illness, (3) to restore health, and (4) to alleviate suffering. Fulfilling these duties requires continual learning, attending workshops and update courses for re-licensing, adapting to social and technological shifts compatibly with client safety and dignity, applying evidence-based care through the nursing process, and safeguarding one's own health and workplace safety. Accountability means being answerable for one's conduct and able to justify clinical judgments. The code identifies four areas of accountability: (a) to society, (b) to the employer under an employment contract, (c) to the client under existing law, and (d) to the profession. Registered nurses bear all four, including professional accountability to act in the client's best interest. Student nurses cannot hold professional accountability because they are not on the professional register, yet remain accountable in the other three areas: if delegated a wound dressing, a student must decline if incompetent and is answerable for any harm caused, while the delegating registered nurse retains professional accountability for ensuring proper materials and verifying the student's competence.

content.heading: Practical Application of the Client's Bill of Rights in Nursing Care
content.body: Translating client rights into bedside practice requires using the nursing process to assess, diagnose, plan, implement, and evaluate equitable care while upholding client dignity. Nurses must respect cultural, customary, and spiritual beliefs without imposing personal values—educating clients gently to reconsider beliefs only when they endanger health. Nurses safeguard participation and confidentiality by explaining options, checking baseline understanding, correcting misconceptions, and never sharing private disclosures without consent unless strictly necessary. When delegating self-care tasks to clients, nurses match expectations to current acuity: during acute illness, the nurse performs tasks the client lacks strength for—conserving energy for vital functions like respiration and digestion—and gradually restores client participation during recovery to foster self-reliance. Nurses must also recognize their own competency limits to prevent harm and liability, collaborate courteously with co-workers, and intervene decisively—first alerting a failing colleague and escalating if needed—whenever client safety is endangered.

inTextQuestions.question: How do the consequences of violating a legal right differ from violating an ethical right?
inTextQuestions.answer: Violating a legal right can subject a person to civil or criminal liability enforced by law, whereas violating an ethical right results in professional sanctions such as reprimand, censure, suspension, or expulsion from the profession.

inTextQuestions.question: What are the four fundamental responsibilities of nurses outlined in the ICN Code of Ethics?
inTextQuestions.answer: To promote health, to prevent illness, to restore health, and to alleviate suffering.

inTextQuestions.question: Why can a student nurse not be held professionally accountable, and what accountability does a student still carry when delegated a wound dressing?
inTextQuestions.answer: Student nurses are not yet entered on the professional register so they lack professional accountability, but they remain accountable to society, the employer/institution, and the client under law—meaning they must refuse tasks beyond their competence and are answerable for harm caused, while the delegating RN retains professional accountability.

inTextQuestions.question: Under what exceptions may confidential health information be disclosed without a client's written permission?
inTextQuestions.answer: Upon court order, as required by law (e.g., mandatory reporting of certain communicable diseases or child abuse), or when necessary in clinical judgment to protect the client or others from physical danger.

saqs.question: Define 'right' and 'obligation', and differentiate legal rights from ethical rights in health care delivery.
saqs.answer: A right is a claim to a particular privilege, and an obligation is willingness to accept the burden of a duty for its rewards or risks. Legal rights are entitlements within law co-existing with binding legal obligations whose breach triggers civil or criminal liability; ethical rights impose moral duties on professionals without statutory enforcement, whose breach leads to professional reprimand, censure, suspension, or expulsion.

saqs.question: Summarize the six Principles of Patients' Rights approved by the National Health Council Board of Directors (1995).
saqs.answer: Patients have the right to: (1) informed consent, timely specialty access, second opinions, confidentiality, and respect for advance directives; (2) concise, clear health coverage information; (3) know how coverage payment decisions are made and how to appeal fairly; (4) complete cost information for coverage and care; (5) reasonable choice of providers and provider credentials; and (6) know provider financial incentives or clinical restrictions affecting practice.

saqs.question: List the four overarching responsibilities of patients in health care and identify five of the nine principal areas of a Patients' Bill of Rights.
saqs.answer: Patients' four responsibilities are: pursuing healthy lifestyles, becoming knowledgeable about their health plans, actively participating in health care decisions, and cooperating with mutually accepted courses of treatment. Five principal Bill of Rights areas include information disclosure, choice of providers and plans, access to emergency services, participation in treatment, and confidentiality of health information (others: respect/non-discrimination, complaints, consumer responsibilities, full copy).

saqs.question: Identify the four areas of accountability for nurses and explain how accountability is shared when a registered nurse delegates a task to a student nurse.
saqs.answer: The four areas are accountability to society, to the employer under a contract of employment, to the client under existing law, and to the profession. When delegating a wound dressing to a student, the student holds the first three accountabilities and must refuse if incompetent, while the registered nurse retains professional accountability for ensuring proper materials and verifying the student's competence.

saqs.question: Explain how a nurse applies the Client's Bill of Rights regarding cultural beliefs, graded client participation during illness, and unsafe co-worker conduct.
saqs.answer: The nurse respects client values and customs without imposing personal beliefs, educating gently if a belief harms health; performs care for acutely ill clients to conserve energy for vital functions before gradually involving them as they recover to promote self-reliance; and safeguards clients endangered by a co-worker by addressing the lapse directly and escalating if improvement does not occur.
